title: Evaluate Division Queries
pattern: weighted graph DFS with a precomputed adjacency map
statement:
A set of unit conversions is given. `equations[i]` is a list of variable names, and `values[i]` is the integer ratio it states. Only the first two names of a row carry a conversion: when a row names at least two variables, the first divided by the second equals `values[i]`. A row that names fewer than two variables states no conversion at all, although every name it mentions is still a known variable.

Only the first `min(equations.length, values.length)` rows are backed by a value; a row past that point states no conversion either.

A row whose value is `0` says that the first name is zero of the second, which can be multiplied by but not divided by: such a row is read forwards as usual and contributes nothing in the reverse direction, because no name is obtained by dividing by zero.

Answer every query. `queries[j]` is a list of variable names and only its first two entries are read: it asks for the ratio of `queries[j][0]` to `queries[j][1]`. A query row naming fewer than two variables is answered `-1`. Return `-1` as well when the ratio cannot be determined, which happens whenever a name is unknown or the two names are not connected by the stated conversions. A row whose two names are the same variable is answered `1` exactly when that name is known.

Conversions are walked one step at a time: from the current name, take the first row in order that relates it to a name not yet visited on this walk, multiplying by `values[i]` when the row is read forwards (`current / other == values[i]`) and dividing by it when the row is read backwards. The first such walk that reaches the target name supplies the answer, so rows that contradict each other are resolved in row order rather than rejected.

Every variable name is a lowercase English word, and all query answers are ordinary JSON numbers.

Constraints: `1 <= equations.length <= 100`, `1 <= values.length <= 100`, `0 <= values[i] <= 100`, `1 <= queries.length <= 100`.

constraints: Function signature: `function solve(equations: string[][], values: number[], queries: string[][])`.
Inputs are JSON-serializable values satisfying the bounds stated above.
hints: Each row is one edge of a graph with a weight, and the same edge also exists in the opposite direction carrying the reciprocal weight. A query is a walk from one name to the other.
Only the first two names of a row are read, and a row only carries its ratio while `values` still has an entry for that position. Skip anything shorter or past the end of `values`.
Building the neighbour lists once, instead of rescanning every row at every name, removes a factor of e per query, and a visited set keeps a contradictory cycle from being walked twice.

editorial.approach: Every stated row ties two names together with a ratio, so the conversions form a weighted graph: row `i` gives an edge carrying `values[i]` one way and its reciprocal the other. A query is a walk between two names that multiplies the ratios it crosses. The brute force answers each query on its own by rescanning every row at every name it reaches, multiplying or dividing as it goes, which costs O(q * v * e). The optimal solution builds the neighbour lists once and then walks those lists, so each row is touched a constant number of times per query and the total drops to O(q * (v + e)).
editorial.why_optimal: A query cannot be answered without visiting the names on the route between its two names, and the adjacency map touches each row a constant number of times during that visit, which is the factor of e the precomputation removes. A visited set stops a walk from looping back on itself, so a query never costs more than one pass over its connected part. With q, v and e each capped at 100 the brute force still finishes comfortably, which is why it is an honest baseline rather than a slow outlier.
editorial.pitfalls: Indexing a row past its end: rows are name lists of any length, so only the first two entries may be read and short rows must be skipped. Treating `values` as exactly as long as `equations`, when only the first `min(equations.length, values.length)` rows carry a value. Multiplying by the stated value when a row has to be read backwards instead of dividing by it (or the reverse). Answering `1` for a query whose two names are equal but never appear in any row, since a self-query is only `1` when the name is known. Returning `-1.0` from Python while the JavaScript side returns `-1`, which the judge compares as raw JSON, so the routes that end in a whole number must be reported as integers in both languages.
